title: Joseph of Cupertino (18 September)
hookLine: a slow student whose prayer was so intense that stories say he floated, patron of exam takers

lines: TAKEN IN, TO WORK THE STABLE.
cards: Who gets turned away by a religious order? Joseph of Cupertino did, the story goes. A poor boy from a small town in southern Italy.
Slow at his lessons. Clumsy. So lost in his head that people teased him for his mouth hanging open.
He asked the friars to take him, and they sent him away. When he was finally let in, it was to work in the stable.
Today, the saint students pray to before a test, which has a joke folded inside it: in the stories, Joseph is bad at tests.

teach.b: The stable worker kept praying, and over time the friars saw what was in him and let him study for the priesthood. Study did not go well. Here's the story Catholics tell.
At one exam, the examiner opened the Gospel and asked him about a single passage, and it was the one text he knew well. He passed.

At the next, the story goes, the first candidates answered so well that the bishop passed the rest of the group without questioning them, and Joseph was in that group. That's why students ask his prayers before exams.
Stories say that when Joseph prayed, especially at Mass, joy would seize him and he would rise off the ground. People came to see. Church authorities questioned him.
His superiors, uneasy with the crowds, moved him to quiet friaries, out of sight. Catholics hold the floating stories in different ways. What they honor him for is his humility and his prayer.
Underneath it all is Luke's Gospel.
Jesus rejoices and thanks his Father for hiding these things from the wise and prudent, and the Douay-Rheims finishes the line: "and hast revealed them to little ones."
Joseph was a little one: not clever, not polished, but his prayer was so whole that, in the stories, it lifted him.
He's patron of exams not because he was smart, but because he wasn't, and he was carried through anyway.
For Catholics, a prayer before a test isn't a trick for grades. It's someone small asking for help.

how: Catholics keep the memory of Saint Joseph of Cupertino on 18 September, and students ask his prayers before exams; Franciscans honor him as one of their own.

practice: Bring to mind one person learning something hard right now, a child with homework, a teenager facing finals, a friend studying for a license, and think of the test in front of them, and the nerves.
If you pray, ask Saint Joseph of Cupertino to pray for them; if you don't, hold them in mind and wish them a steady head.

wordCard.voice: Little ones, Jesus's phrase for people like Joseph of Cupertino: the slow, poor student, taken in to work the stable, whose prayer stories say lifted him off the ground. Patron of exams.

orig.note: Greek: an infant, a little one. in Luke 10:21 Jesus thanks the Father for revealing these things to them.
